items.prompt:
A colleague runs a nudging script on five points with step 0.01. It stops at $w = 1.48$, $b = 1.36$ with MSE 0.0608, and they write: “The error stopped falling, so I have the best line.”

(a) What does the script's stop really tell us? (b) Use the numbers from l7 to show that their claim is false here. (c) Suggest two things they could try, and say what each one can and cannot promise. (d) Even with the best line on these five points, what would you still need before trusting it on new data?
items.model:
**(a)** The script stops when a whole round changes nothing. That means none of the four single nudges, $w \pm 0.01$ or $b \pm 0.01$, lowers the MSE. It says nothing about moves it never tries.

**(b)** From (1.48, 1.36): $w + 0.01$ gives 0.0611, $w - 0.01$ gives 0.0627, and $b \pm 0.01$ both give 0.0609. All are above 0.0608, so the script stops. But moving both at once, to (1.49, 1.35), gives 0.0606, lower. And the line $y = 1.5x + 1.3$ has MSE 0.06, which step 0.1 reached. So 0.0608 is not the best.

**(c)** First, try a different step, such as 0.1: here it reaches 0.06, but in general a different step can also stop early, and smaller is not always better (step 0.5 stopped at 0.1). Second, add moves of both numbers together, as in the homework: it reached 0.0602 here, better than 0.0608 but still not 0.06. Each rule can only promise that none of its own moves helps.

**(d)** Fitting five points well is a training score. I would want points kept back, scored once, before trusting the line on new data (l4).

rubric.text: Says the stop means no single nudge of that step lowers the error, not that the line is best
Shows a better line exists: the paired move (0.0606) or $y = 1.5x + 1.3$ (0.06)
Suggests two remedies (another step, paired moves) and says neither guarantees the best line
Notes that even the best fit is a training score and needs kept-back data
